concept.title: Sperner's Lemma Implies Nash Equilibria: Combinatorial Fixed Points in Game Theory
concept.concept_description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. This is a combinatorial analog of Brouwer's fixed point theorem. Nash's theorem states that every finite game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, proved using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Conjecture: Sperner's lemma directly implies Nash's theorem. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.

Define Sperner coloring c: Delta -> {1, ..., n} by c(v) = i where i = argmax_j BR_i(v)_j (player i's best response to v has highest probability on strategy j). Boundary condition: if v is on the face where p_i = 0, then c(v) != i (a player with zero probability cannot have a best response there). Wait, the correct boundary condition is: if v is on the face where v_i = 0, then c(v) is not i. Sperner's lemma: there exists at least one fully colored simplex (with all colors 1, ..., n). The center of this simplex is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium where epsilon depends on the mesh size of the triangulation. As mesh -> 0, epsilon -> 0, giving an exact Nash equilibrium. Algorithm: triangulate Delta with mesh epsilon, color vertices by best responses, find fully colored simplex by Sperner's lemma (using the path-following algorithm). Complexity: O((1/epsilon)^{n-1} * |S|) per iteration. Test: implement for 2x2 games (Matching Pennies, Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes). Verify that the algorithm finds the unique Nash equilibrium.

concept.title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them
concept.concept_description: Formalize a focused finite-space reconstruction theorem on a finite type α using only existing mathlib topology/order interfaces, and avoid any broad equivalence-of-categories claims. The target should be a single clean file proving three concrete statements: (1) for any topology t on α, every open set is downward closed for the specialization relation (`b ⤳ a` and `a ∈ s` imply `b ∈ s`); (2) if α is finite, then every subset that is downward closed under specialization is open, using the existing Alexandrov-discrete instance for finite spaces together with the characterization of open sets by lower sets; (3) on a finite type, two topologies with pointwise equivalent specialization relations are equal because they have the same open sets via (1) and (2). Optional stretch goals are to identify the specialization relation of `Topology.lowerSet` with the underlying preorder and prove the finite inverse statement that reconstructing from specialization gives back the original topology. The file should contain only complete, type-checking declarations, no unrelated material, and theorem names/docstrings aligned with mathlib conventions.
concept.mathematical_framing: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see. Like quantum mechanics, measurement changes the topology. Test: prove that R with the standard topology is the intersection of the lower limit topology and the upper limit topology (2 observers). Prove that the Zariski topology on R^2 requires at least 3 observers. Impact: a new notion of topology where the space itself depends on the observer — the mathematical formalization of 'reality depends on the observer'.
concept.lean_guess: Define a phantom topology as a function T: O -> Top(X) from a set of observers to topologies on X. Define the intersection topology T_cap = intersection of all T(o). Prove: every second-countable T_0 space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with |O| = 2. Proof: for a basis {B_n}, define T(o1) as the topology generated by {B_n : n odd} union {X} and T(o2) by {B_n : n even} union {X}. Then T_cap = tau. Prove non-metrizable spaces need >= 3 observers: the Zariski topology on R^2 cannot be written as the intersection of two first-countable topologies. Test: verify the R example and construct the 3-observer phantom representation for the Zariski topology.

-- NEW_FILE: 5884df3d_retry2_aristotle/Catalog/Geometry/FiniteSpecialization.lean
/-
# Finite reconstruction from the specialization relation

This file develops the *finite reconstruction theorem*: on a finite type, a
topology is completely determined by its specialization relation `⤳`.

We work with mathlib's existing notions throughout:

* `x ⤳ y` is `Specializes x y` (`x` specializes to `y`, i.e. `𝓝 x ≤ 𝓝 y`).
* Finite types are automatically Alexandrov-discrete
  (`Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete`), which is what powers the converse direction.
* The "topology generated by a preorder" is mathlib's lower set topology
  `Topology.lowerSet`, whose open sets are exactly the lower sets.  With this
  convention the specialization relation matches the order directly:
  `a ⤳ b ↔ a ≤ b` (`Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le`).

## Main results

* `isOpen_specializes_down` : every open set is downward closed under
  specialization (valid for an arbitrary topology).
* `isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite` : on a finite type the converse holds, so
  openness is *characterized* by being downward closed under specialization.
* `topology_eq_of_specializes_iff_finite` : **the main deliverable** — two
  topologies on a finite type with the same specialization relation are equal.
* `specializes_preorderTopology_iff` : the specialization relation of the lower
  set topology of a preorder recovers the preorder exactly.
* `specPreorder_lowerSet_eq` / `lowerSet_specPreorder_eq_finite` : a pair of
  inverse theorems on finite spaces.

## Sanity checks

* `specializes_discrete_iff` : the discrete topology has trivial specialization.
* `specPreorder_lowerSet_eq` : the lower set topology recovers its preorder.
-/

import Mathlib

open Topology

namespace FiniteSpecialization

variable {α : Type*}

/-! ### Goal 1: open sets are downward closed under specialization -/

/-- For an arbitrary topology, every open set is downward closed under
specialization: if `a ∈ s` and `b ⤳ a` then `b ∈ s`.

This is exactly `IsOpen.stableUnderGeneralization`, restated in the requested
shape using `specializes_iff_forall_open`. -/
theorem isOpen_specializes_down {t : TopologicalSpace α} {s : Set α}
    (hs : IsOpen s) : ∀ ⦃a b⦄, a ∈ s → b ⤳ a → b ∈ s :=
  fun _ _ ha hba => (specializes_iff_forall_open.mp hba) s hs ha

/-! ### Goal 2: the finite converse -/

/-- **Characterization of openness on a finite type.**  A set `s` is open iff it
is downward closed under specialization.

The forward direction is `isOpen_specializes_down`; the converse uses that finite
types are Alexandrov-discrete (`Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete`), where openness is
equivalent to stability under generalization
(`isOpen_iff_forall_specializes`).  The minimal open neighborhood of a point `a`
referenced in the informal strategy is mathlib's `nhdsKer {a}`, the kernel of the
neighborhood filter, i.e. the intersection of all open neighborhoods of `a`. -/
theorem isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite [Fintype α] [TopologicalSpace α]
    (s : Set α) : IsOpen s ↔ ∀ ⦃a b⦄, a ∈ s → b ⤳ a → b ∈ s := by
  rw [isOpen_iff_forall_specializes]
  exact ⟨fun h a b ha hba => h b a hba ha, fun h x y hxy hy => h hy hxy⟩

/-! ### Goal 3: extensionality from specialization (main deliverable) -/

/-- **Finite reconstruction theorem.**  Two topologies on a finite type that have
the same specialization relation pointwise are equal.

The proof is extensionality on open sets: by
`isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite` openness of a set under either topology is
characterized purely by the specialization relation, which agrees by hypothesis. -/
theorem topology_eq_of_specializes_iff_finite [Fintype α] (t₁ t₂ : TopologicalSpace α)
    (h : ∀ a b : α, (@Specializes α t₁ a b ↔ @Specializes α t₂ a b)) : t₁ = t₂ := by
  haveI : @AlexandrovDiscrete α t₁ := @Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete α t₁ _
  haveI : @AlexandrovDiscrete α t₂ := @Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete α t₂ _
  apply TopologicalSpace.ext
  ext s
  rw [@isOpen_iff_forall_specializes α t₁ _ s, @isOpen_iff_forall_specializes α t₂ _ s]
  exact ⟨fun H x y hxy hy => H x y ((h x y).mpr hxy) hy,
         fun H x y hxy hy => H x y ((h x y).mp hxy) hy⟩

/-! ### Goal 4: the preorder topology recovers the preorder -/

/-- The specialization relation of the lower set topology of a preorder recovers
the order exactly.

Orientation note: with mathlib's lower set topology (open sets = lower sets) the
specialization relation satisfies `a ⤳ b ↔ a ≤ b`
(`Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le`).  (For the *upper* set topology, used
by mathlib's `specializationPreorder`, the convention is reversed:
`a ⤳ b ↔ b ≤ a`.) -/
theorem specializes_preorderTopology_iff [Preorder α] (a b : α) :
    @Specializes α (Topology.lowerSet α) a b ↔ a ≤ b := by
  letI := Topology.lowerSet α
  haveI : Topology.IsLowerSet α := ⟨rfl⟩
  exact Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le

/-! ### Sanity check -/

/-- Sanity check: the discrete topology has trivial specialization. -/
theorem specializes_discrete_iff [TopologicalSpace α] [DiscreteTopology α] (a b : α) :

# Chip-Firing and Divisor Theory on a Finite Graph — Definitions

This file lays the *load-bearing foundation* of Baker–Norine divisor theory on a finite
graph, working entirely over an ordinary Mathlib `SimpleGraph V`.

The central object is the **graph Laplacian** (chip-firing operator)

  `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`,

a map `(V → ℤ) → Divisor V`.  We record here the definitions (`Divisor`, `lap`,
`divisorDegree`, `genus`, `canonicalDivisor`, `Effective`, `singleVertexDivisor`,
`bnNumber`) together with the *homomorphism layer*: `lap` is additive, kills constants,
respects negation, and lands in degree zero.  These five facts are exactly the axioms
needed to make chip-firing (linear) equivalence an `Equivalence` and degree a class
invariant (developed in `Tropical.ChipFiring.Theorems`).

## References

* Baker, M. and Norine, S. "Riemann–Roch and Abel–Jacobi theory on a finite graph" (2007)

-- !-- Lab Notebook -- !--
Hypothesis: The whole algebraic layer of divisor theory is the *coset relation of one
  homomorphism* `lap`.  If `lap` is an additive, constant-killing, degree-zero map then
  linear equivalence and its degree invariance must follow purely formally.
Result: Confirmed.  `lap_zero`/`lap_neg`/`lap_add` are literally the three
  equivalence-relation axioms; `lap_deg_zero` is literally degree invariance.
Insight: `lap_deg_zero` needs *no* handshake/degree counting — it is pure antisymmetry of
  `f v − f u` under the symmetric adjacency relation, witnessed by a single
  `Finset.sum_nbij'` swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` that negates every summand.
Failure analysis: Earlier encodings (a weighted multigraph `V → V → ℤ` carrying explicit
  symmetry, and a `deg(v)·f v − ∑ f u` Laplacian) obscured the antisymmetry that does all
  the work; the clean `∑_{u∼v}(f v − f u)` form makes the swap argument immediate.
-- !-- end -- !--
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset BigOperators SimpleGraph

/-! ## Divisors -/

/-- A divisor on a graph with vertex set `V` is an integer-valued function on vertices
(a formal `ℤ`-linear combination of vertices). -/
structure Divisor (V : Type*) where
  coeff : V → ℤ

namespace Divisor
variable {V : Type*}

@[ext] lemma ext {D E : Divisor V} (h : D.coeff = E.coeff) : D = E := by
  cases D; cases E; simpa using h

instance : Zero (Divisor V) := ⟨⟨fun _ => 0⟩⟩
instance : Add (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v + E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Neg (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D => ⟨fun v => -D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Sub (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v - E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℕ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℤ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩

@[simp] lemma zero_coeff (v : V) : (0 : Divisor V).coeff v = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma add_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D + E).coeff v = D.coeff v + E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma neg_coeff (D : Divisor V) (v : V) : (-D).coeff v = -D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma sub_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D - E).coeff v = D.coeff v - E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma nsmul_coeff (n : ℕ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma zsmul_coeff (n : ℤ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl

/-- The coefficient projection `Divisor V → (V → ℤ)` is injective; hence divisors form an
additive commutative group under pointwise operations. -/
instance : AddCommGroup (Divisor V) :=
  Function.Injective.addCommGroup (Divisor.coeff)
    (fun _ _ h => Divisor.ext h)
    rfl (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)
    (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)

end Divisor

/-- A divisor is **effective** when every coefficient is non-negative. -/
def Effective {V : Type*} (D : Divisor V) : Prop := ∀ v, 0 ≤ D.coeff v

/-! ## Degree -/

section Degree
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V]

/-- The **degree** of a divisor is the sum of its coefficients. -/
def divisorDegree (D : Divisor V) : ℤ := ∑ v, D.coeff v

@[simp] lemma divisorDegree_zero : divisorDegree (0 : Divisor V) = 0 := by
  simp [divisorDegree]

lemma divisorDegree_add (D E : Divisor V) :
    divisorDegree (D + E) = divisorDegree D + divisorDegree E := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_add_distrib]

lemma divisorDegree_neg (D : Divisor V) : divisorDegree (-D) = -divisorDegree D := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_neg_distrib]

end Degree

/-! ## The graph Laplacian (chip-firing operator) -/

section Laplacian
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- The graph Laplacian applied to a firing pattern `f : V → ℤ`.  Firing along `f` moves
chips according to `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`. -/
def lap (f : V → ℤ) : Divisor V := ⟨fun v => ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u)⟩

@[simp] lemma lap_coeff (f : V → ℤ) (v : V) :
    (lap G f).coeff v = ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u) := rfl

-- !-- The empty firing pattern moves no chips: each summand `0 - 0` vanishes. -- !--
@[simp] theorem lap_zero : lap G (0 : V → ℤ) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- A constant firing pattern is in the kernel: every summand `c - c` vanishes. -- !--
theorem lap_const (c : ℤ) : lap G (fun _ => c) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- Additivity: `(f+g)v - (f+g)u = (f v - f u) + (g v - g u)`, then split the sum. -- !--
theorem lap_add (f g : V → ℤ) : lap G (f + g) = lap G f + lap G g := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.add_coeff, Pi.add_apply, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Negation: `lap` is `ℤ`-linear, so it commutes with pointwise negation. -- !--
theorem lap_neg (f : V → ℤ) : lap G (-f) = - lap G f := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.neg_coeff, Pi.neg_apply, ← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Every Laplacian has degree zero, by antisymmetry of `f v - f u` under the symmetric
--     adjacency relation: the swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` on adjacent ordered pairs negates each
--     summand yet preserves the index set, forcing `X = -X`. -- !--
theorem lap_deg_zero (f : V → ℤ) : divisorDegree (lap G f) = 0 := by
  unfold divisorDegree
  simp only [lap_coeff]
  have key : (∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u))
      = ∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f u - f v) := by
    rw [Finset.sum_sigma', Finset.sum_sigma']
    apply Finset.sum_nbij' (fun x => (⟨x.2, x.1⟩ : Σ _ : V, V)) (fun x => ⟨x.2, x.1⟩)
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl
  have hneg : (∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f u - f v))
      = -(∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u)) := by
    rw [← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]; apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro v _
    rw [← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]; apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring
  have := key.trans hneg
  linarith

/-! ## Genus and the canonical divisor -/

/-- The (combinatorial) **genus** of a graph: `g = |E| − |V| + 1`, the first Betti number. -/
def genus : ℤ := (G.edgeFinset.card : ℤ) - (Fintype.card V : ℤ) + 1

/-- The **canonical divisor** assigns to each vertex `deg(v) − 2`. -/
def canonicalDivisor : Divisor V := ⟨fun v => (G.degree v : ℤ) - 2⟩

end Laplacian

/-! ## Single-vertex divisors -/

section Single
variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V]

/-- The divisor `k·[v₀]` placing `k` chips on `v₀` and none elsewhere. -/
def singleVertexDivisor (v₀ : V) (k : ℤ) : Divisor V :=
  ⟨fun w => if w = v₀ then k else 0⟩

end Single

/-! ## The Brill–Noether number -/

/-- The **Brill–Noether number** `ρ(g,r,d) = g − (r+1)(g − d + r)`. -/
def bnNumber (g r d : ℤ) : ℤ := g - (r + 1) * (g - d + r)

# Summary of changes for run 84becd05-0dac-4116-91e5-3f77f178924f
Created a finished, self-contained Lean file `Catalog/Geometry/FiniteSpecialization.lean` proving the finite reconstruction theorem from the specialization relation. It compiles cleanly against the project's mathlib with no `sorry` and no extra axioms, reusing mathlib's existing machinery throughout.

Orientation note: I determined from mathlib that for the lower-set topology the convention is `a ⤳ b ↔ a ≤ b` (`Topology.IsLowerSet.specializes_iff_le`), so I used the lower-set topology as the "topology generated by a preorder" and stated everything accordingly.

Contents (theorem names reflect what is proved):

1. `isOpen_specializes_down` — for an arbitrary topology, every open set is downward closed under specialization: `IsOpen s → ∀ ⦃a b⦄, a ∈ s → b ⤳ a → b ∈ s` (a restatement of mathlib's `IsOpen.stableUnderGeneralization`).

2. `isOpen_iff_specializes_down_finite` — on a `Fintype`, the converse holds, characterizing openness as being downward closed under specialization. The proof uses that finite types are Alexandrov-discrete (`Finite.toAlexandrovDiscrete`), where the relevant minimal-neighborhood construction is mathlib's `nhdsKer {a}`, giving `isOpen_iff_forall_specializes`.

3. `topology_eq_of_specializes_iff_finite` — the main deliverable: two topologies on a finite type with the same pointwise specialization relation are equal, proved by extensionality on open sets via the characterization in (2).

4. `specializes_preorderTopology_iff` — the specialization relation of the lower-set topology of a preorder recovers the order exactly (`a ⤳ b ↔ a ≤ b`).

5. A pair of inverse theorems on finite spaces (no bundled equivalence, per the request): `specPreorder_lowerSet_eq` (preorder → topology → preorder) and `lowerSet_specPreorder_eq_finite` (topology → preorder → topology), built on a small `specPreorder` definition.

Sanity check: `specializes_discrete_iff` shows the discrete topology has trivial specialization (`a ⤳ b ↔ a = b`).

I verified the file elaborates with exit code 0 (`lake env lean` against the project's mathlib) and contains no `sorry`. # FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Phantom Topologies (Combinatorics)

Cycle-1/2 results live in `Catalog/Speculative/PhantomTopologies.lean`, where we proved that
on a finite carrier the topology is a *phantom* of its specialization preorder:

- `topology_eq_of_specializes_iff` — a topology is determined by the bare `⤳` relation;
- `specPreorder_bijective` — `topology ↦ specialization preorder` is a **bijection**
  `TopologicalSpace α ≃ Preorder α` (the classical "finite spaces = preorders");
- `continuous_iff_specializes` — continuity *is* specialization-monotonicity (morphisms are
  phantoms too);
- `phantom_asymmetry` — the realized preorders are genuinely directional.

The conjectures below are bold, falsifiable next steps. Each comes with a concrete Lean target.

---

## C1. T0 rigidity: phantoms collapse exactly onto partial orders
**Conjecture.** The observation map `specPreorder` restricts to a bijection between the
`T0` topologies on a finite `α` and the **partial orders** on `α`.
**Why plausible.** `specializationOrder` already upgrades the preorder to a partial order under
`T0Space`; antisymmetry is exactly the `T0` (Kolmogorov) condition.
**Lean target.**
```
theorem specPreorder_T0_bijective [Finite α] :
    Function.Bijective
      (fun (t : {t : TopologicalSpace α // @T0Space α t}) => (specialization partial order))
```
A corollary would be a *counting* statement: `#{T0 topologies on Fin n} = #{partial orders on Fin n}`
(OEIS A001035), complementing the full count A000798.

## C2. Homeomorphism is an order-isomorphism of phantoms
**Conjecture.** For finite spaces, `Homeomorph α β` is in natural bijection with order-isomorphisms
of their specialization preorders: `(α ≃ₜ β) ≃ (Specialization α ≃o Specialization β)`.
**Why plausible.** `continuous_iff_specializes` gives the arrow-level dictionary; a homeomorphism is
a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, i.e. a monotone bijection with monotone inverse.
**Lean target.** Build the explicit `Equiv` and prove both round-trips; specialize to deduce that
two finite spaces are homeomorphic iff their preorders are order-isomorphic.

## C3. Connectivity is a phantom (combinatorial connectivity)
**Conjecture.** A finite space is topologically connected **iff** its specialization preorder is
connected as a graph under the comparability relation `x ≤ y ∨ y ≤ x` (zigzag-connected).
**Why plausible.** In an Alexandrov space the minimal open set of `x` is its up-set; topological
components match equivalence classes of the reflexive–symmetric–transitive closure of `≤`.
**Lean target.**
```
theorem connected_iff_preorder_connected [Finite α] [TopologicalSpace α] :
    ConnectedSpace α ↔ (∀ x y : α, Relation.ReflTransGen (fun a b => a ⤳ b ∨ b ⤳ a) x y)
```

## C4. McCord/Möbius bridge: Euler characteristic = Möbius number
**Conjecture.** For a finite `T0` space `X` with specialization poset `P`, the reduced Euler
characteristic of the order complex `Δ(P)` equals the Möbius number `μ(P̂)` of `P` with adjoined
`⊥`/`⊤` — a strict identity between a topological invariant and a purely combinatorial one.
**Why plausible.** This is the finite-space shadow of McCord's weak-homotopy equivalence
`|Δ(P)| ≃ X`; the alternating face count of `Δ(P)` is the order-complex Euler characteristic, which
Philip Hall's theorem identifies with a Möbius value.
**Lean target.** Define `orderComplex P` (chains of `P`), its Euler characteristic, and prove the
identity for the partial order produced by `specializationOrder`.

## C5. Asymptotic dominance of asymmetric phantoms
**Conjecture.** The fraction of topologies on `Fin n` that are `T0` (genuinely asymmetric phantoms,
cf. `phantom_asymmetry`) tends to `1` as `n → ∞`; equivalently `A000798(n) / A001035(n) → 1`.
**Why plausible.** A random preorder is asymptotically almost surely a partial order, since the
number of nontrivial inseparability classes is negligible for large `n`.
**Lean target.** A clean intermediate, fully finitary milestone: prove the *exact* small-case
counts agree with the phantom bijection, e.g. that there are exactly `4` topologies and `4`
preorders on a 2-element type, and exactly `3` of them are `T0`, by transporting the count along
`specPreorder_bijective`.

Work with linear maps `d₂ : A →ₗ[K] B` and `d₁ : B →ₗ[K] C` satisfying `d₁.comp d₂ = 0`. Define `cycles := LinearMap.ker d₁` and `boundaries := LinearMap.range d₂`. Then combine these into the additive CSS formula `finrank homology + finrank (LinearMap.range d₂) + finrank (LinearMap.range d₁) = finrank B`, and only afterward derive the subtraction form if the needed `Nat` arithmetic lemmas are straightforward. concept.mathematical_framing: The Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error-correcting codes are constructed from classical linear codes C_1, C_2 with C_2 perp subset C_1. The CSS code encodes dim(C_1) - dim(C_2) logical qubits. This is exactly the definition of a cohomology group: H^1(C_1, C_2) = C_1 / C_2. Conjecture: every CSS code is equivalent to a cohomology computation on a simplicial complex, and vice versa. Specifically, given a simplicial complex K, the CSS code with C_1 = Z_1(K, F_2) (1-cycles) and C_2 = B_1(K, F_2) (1-boundaries) encodes dim(H_1(K, F_2)) logical qubits with distance d = min(length of shortest non-trivial cycle, length of shortest non-trivial cocycle). This is the homological quantum error-correcting code HQECC(K). The distance d equals the systole of K (the length of the shortest non-contractible cycle). Conjecture: for the hypercube Q_n (n-dimensional cube graph), the HQECC encodes 1 qubit with distance d = 2^{n/2} (achieving the quantum Singleton bound). Test: construct HQECC for Q_4, Q_6, Q_8 and verify the parameters. Impact: quantum error correction is cohomology. # Homological core of CSS quantum codes

This file formalizes the finite-dimensional linear-algebraic core of
**CSS (Calderbank–Shor–Steane) quantum error-correcting codes** as the homology
of a two-step chain complex over the field `F = ZMod 2`.

A CSS code is built from a length-3 chain complex of `F`-vector spaces
```
  A --d₂--> B --d₁--> C ,        with   d₁ ∘ d₂ = 0 .
```
The middle space `B` is the space of physical qubits, the map `d₁` encodes the
`Z`-type stabilizers and `d₂` the `X`-type stabilizers.  The *logical qubits* of
the code are exactly the homology
```
  H = ker d₁ / im d₂ ,
```
and the number of logical qubits is `finrank F H`.

The main result (`css_dimension_formula` and its subtraction-normalized form
`css_dimension_formula_sub`) is the standard dimension count
```
  finrank H = finrank B - finrank (range d₁) - finrank (range d₂),
```
equivalently, in the `Nat`-friendly additive form,
```
  finrank H + finrank (range d₂) + finrank (range d₁) = finrank B .
```

## Main definitions

* `cycles d₁`              — `ker d₁`, the `Z`-cycles.
* `boundaries d₂`         — `range d₂`, the `X`-boundaries.
* `boundaryInsideCycles`  — the copy of `boundaries d₂` sitting inside `cycles d₁`,
                            realized as `Submodule.comap (cycles d₁).subtype (boundaries d₂)`.
* `homology`              — `cycles d₁ ⧸ boundaryInsideCycles`.

## Main results

* `boundaries_le_cycles`             — `im d₂ ≤ ker d₁`.
* `finrank_boundaryInsideCycles`     — `finrank boundaryInsideCycles = finrank (range d₂)`.
* `finrank_cycles_add_finrank_range` — `finrank (cycles d₁) + finrank (range d₁) = finrank B`.
* `finrank_homology_add`             — `finrank H + finrank boundaryInsideCycles = finrank (cycles d₁)`.
* `css_dimension_formula`            — the additive CSS dimension formula.
* `css_dimension_formula_sub`        — the subtraction-normalized CSS dimension formula.
-/

import Mathlib

open Module

namespace HomologicalCSS

/-- The base field of a CSS code: the two-element field `ZMod 2`. -/
abbrev F := ZMod 2

variable {A B C : Type*}
  [AddCommGroup A] [Module F A] [FiniteDimensional F A]
  [AddCommGroup B] [Module F B] [FiniteDimensional F B]
  [AddCommGroup C] [Module F C] [FiniteDimensional F C]

/-- The `Z`-cycles of the CSS chain complex: `ker d₁`. -/
def cycles (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C) : Submodule F B := LinearMap.ker d₁

/-- The `X`-boundaries of the CSS chain complex: `range d₂`. -/
def boundaries (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) : Submodule F B := LinearMap.range d₂

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The chain-complex condition `d₁ ∘ d₂ = 0` forces every boundary to be a cycle. -/
theorem boundaries_le_cycles (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)

  LinearMap.range_le_ker_iff.mpr hchain

/-- The boundaries, viewed as a submodule of the cycles, via `comap` of the
inclusion `cycles d₁ ↪ B`.  This presentation is the one matching Mathlib's
`Submodule.comapSubtypeEquivOfLe` and quotient `finrank` lemmas. -/
def boundaryInsideCycles (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)
    (_hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) : Submodule F (cycles d₁) :=
  Submodule.comap (cycles d₁).subtype (boundaries d₂)

/-- The homology `H = ker d₁ / im d₂`: the space of logical qubits.

This is an `abbrev` so that the `AddCommGroup`, `Module`, and `FiniteDimensional`
instances of the underlying quotient module are found by instance resolution. -/
abbrev homology (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C) (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :=
  (cycles d₁) ⧸ boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hchain

/-! ### Finite-dimensionality instances -/

instance (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C) : FiniteDimensional F (cycles d₁) := by
  unfold cycles; infer_instance

instance (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) : FiniteDimensional F (boundaries d₂) := by
  unfold boundaries; infer_instance

instance (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C) (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    FiniteDimensional F (boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hchain) := by
  unfold boundaryInsideCycles; infer_instance

instance (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C) (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    FiniteDimensional F (homology d₂ d₁ hchain) := by
  unfold homology; infer_instance

/-! ### A linear equivalence `boundaryInsideCycles ≃ₗ boundaries` -/

/-- The included boundary submodule is linearly equivalent to `boundaries d₂`. -/
noncomputable def boundaryInsideCyclesEquiv (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)
    (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    (boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hchain) ≃ₗ[F] (boundaries d₂) :=
  Submodule.comapSubtypeEquivOfLe (boundaries_le_cycles d₂ d₁ hchain)

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The finrank of the included boundary submodule equals the finrank of `range d₂`. -/
theorem finrank_boundaryInsideCycles (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)
    (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hchain) = finrank F (LinearMap.range d₂) :=
  (boundaryInsideCyclesEquiv d₂ d₁ hchain).finrank_eq

/-! ### Rank–nullity for the cycles -/

omit [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- Rank–nullity for `d₁`: `finrank (cycles d₁) + finrank (range d₁) = finrank B`. -/
theorem finrank_cycles_add_finrank_range (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C) :
    finrank F (cycles d₁) + finrank F (LinearMap.range d₁) = finrank F B := by
  rw [add_comm]
  exact LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker d₁

/-! ### Quotient-dimension identity for homology -/

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The quotient-dimension identity:
`finrank H + finrank boundaryInsideCycles = finrank (cycles d₁)`. -/
theorem finrank_homology_add (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)
    (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (homology d₂ d₁ hchain) + finrank F (boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hchain)
      = finrank F (cycles d₁) :=
  Submodule.finrank_quotient_add_finrank (boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hchain)

/-! ### The CSS dimension formula -/

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The CSS dimension formula, additive (`Nat`-friendly) form:
`finrank H + finrank (range d₂) + finrank (range d₁) = finrank B`. -/
theorem css_dimension_formula (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)
    (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (homology d₂ d₁ hchain) + finrank F (LinearMap.range d₂)
        + finrank F (LinearMap.range d₁)
      = finrank F B := by
  have h1 := finrank_homology_add d₂ d₁ hchain
  have h2 := finrank_cycles_add_finrank_range d₁
  have h3 := finrank_boundaryInsideCycles d₂ d₁ hchain
  omega

omit [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F C] in
/-- The CSS dimension formula, subtraction-normalized form:
`finrank H = finrank B - finrank (range d₁) - finrank (range d₂)`. -/
theorem css_dimension_formula_sub (d₂ : A →ₗ[F] B) (d₁ : B →ₗ[F] C)
    (hchain : d₁.comp d₂ = 0) :
    finrank F (homology d₂ d₁ hchain)
      = finrank F B - finrank F (LinearMap.range d₁) - finrank F (LinearMap.range d₂) := by
  have h := css_dimension_formula d₂ d₁ hchain
  omega

end HomologicalCSS

namespace Retrocausal

/-! ## Part I. The temporal excluded middle (TEM) -/

/-- **Temporal excluded middle.** In *every* Heyting algebra the *double negation* of
the law of excluded middle holds: `¬¬(a ∨ ¬a) = ⊤`. Intuitionistically LEM may fail,
but its temporal (doubly-negated) shadow always survives — effects may precede causes
without contradiction. -/
theorem temporal_excluded_middle {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α] (a : α) :
    (a ⊔ aᶜ)ᶜᶜ = ⊤ := by
  have h : (a ⊔ aᶜ)ᶜ = ⊥ := by rw [compl_sup_distrib, inf_compl_eq_bot]
  rw [h, compl_bot]

/-- **LEM ⟺ double-negation elimination.** The law of excluded middle holds for every
element iff double negation can be eliminated for every element. Hence *rejecting* LEM is
equivalent to *rejecting* DNE: any logic without LEM is genuinely intuitionistic.

The backward direction reuses `temporal_excluded_middle`: DNE turns the always-valid
doubly-negated LEM back into honest LEM. -/
theorem lem_iff_dne {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α] :
    (∀ a : α, a ⊔ aᶜ = ⊤) ↔ (∀ a : α, aᶜᶜ = a) := by
  constructor
  · intro hlem a
    have hd : aᶜᶜ ⊓ (a ⊔ aᶜ) = (aᶜᶜ ⊓ a) ⊔ (aᶜᶜ ⊓ aᶜ) := inf_sup_left _ _ _
    rw [hlem a, inf_top_eq] at hd
    have h2 : aᶜᶜ ⊓ aᶜ = ⊥ := by rw [inf_comm]; exact inf_compl_eq_bot
    rw [h2, sup_bot_eq, inf_comm, inf_eq_left.mpr le_compl_compl] at hd
    exact hd
  · intro hdne a
    have h : (a ⊔ aᶜ)ᶜᶜ = ⊤ := temporal_excluded_middle a
    rw [hdne] at h; exact h

/-- **Retrocausal logic must be intuitionistic (contrapositive form).** If LEM fails for
some element, then double-negation elimination must fail for some element too. -/
theorem lem_fails_of_dne_fails {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α]
    (h : ∃ a : α, aᶜᶜ ≠ a) : ∃ a : α, a ⊔ aᶜ ≠ ⊤ := by
  by_contra hc
  push_neg at hc
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h
  exact ha (lem_iff_dne.mp hc a)

/-- **Concrete failure of LEM.** The three-element chain `Fin 3` is a genuinely
non-Boolean Heyting algebra: for the middle element `1`, `1 ⊔ 1ᶜ = 1 ≠ ⊤`. This is the
existence witness backing the abstract `lem_fails_of_dne_fails`. -/
theorem retro_lem_fails : ∃ a : Fin 3, a ⊔ aᶜ ≠ ⊤ := ⟨1, by decide⟩

/-- The temporal excluded middle nevertheless holds at that same witness in `Fin 3`. -/
theorem retro_tem_holds : ((1 : Fin 3) ⊔ (1 : Fin 3)ᶜ)ᶜᶜ = ⊤ :=
  temporal_excluded_middle 1

/-! ## Part II. Retrocausal time-reversal -/

/-- A **retrocausal time-reversal** on a Heyting algebra is an order-*reversing*
involution `rev`. Order reversal encodes "implications flowing backward in time":
`a ≤ b` (cause `a` entails effect `b`) becomes `rev b ≤ rev a` under time reversal.
Involutivity is the algebraic shadow of the CPT theorem (`(CPT)² = id`). -/
class RetrocausalHeyting (α : Type*) [HeytingAlgebra α] where
  /-- The time-reversal / CPT operator. -/
  rev : α → α
  /-- Time reversal is an involution: applying it twice is the identity. -/
  rev_involutive : Function.Involutive rev
  /-- Time reversal reverses entailment (implications flow backward). -/
  rev_antitone : ∀ {a b : α}, a ≤ b → rev b ≤ rev a

export RetrocausalHeyting (rev rev_involutive rev_antitone)

variable {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α] [RetrocausalHeyting α]

/-- Time reversal sends contradiction to tautology: `rev ⊥ = ⊤`. -/
theorem rev_bot : rev (⊥ : α) = ⊤ := by
  apply top_le_iff.mp
  have h := rev_antitone (bot_le : (⊥ : α) ≤ rev ⊤)
  rwa [rev_involutive ⊤] at h

/-- Time reversal sends tautology to contradiction: `rev ⊤ = ⊥`. -/
theorem rev_top : rev (⊤ : α) = ⊥ := by
  apply le_bot_iff.mp
  have h := rev_antitone (le_top : rev ⊥ ≤ (⊤ : α))
  rwa [rev_involutive ⊥] at h

/-- **De Morgan for time-reversal.** A retrocausal involution turns joins into meets:
`rev (a ⊔ b) = rev a ⊓ rev b`. -/
theorem rev_sup (a b : α) : rev (a ⊔ b) = rev a ⊓ rev b := by
  apply le_antisymm
  · exact le_inf (rev_antitone le_sup_left) (rev_antitone le_sup_right)
  · have h1 : a ≤ rev (rev a ⊓ rev b) := by
      have h := rev_antitone (inf_le_left : rev a ⊓ rev b ≤ rev a)
      rwa [rev_involutive a] at h
    have h2 : b ≤ rev (rev a ⊓ rev b) := by
      have h := rev_antitone (inf_le_right : rev a ⊓ rev b ≤ rev b)
      rwa [rev_involutive b] at h
    have h3 := rev_antitone (sup_le h1 h2)
    rwa [rev_involutive (rev a ⊓ rev b)] at h3

/-- **Dual De Morgan for time-reversal.** A retrocausal involution turns meets into
joins: `rev (a ⊓ b) = rev a ⊔ rev b`. -/
theorem rev_inf (a b : α) : rev (a ⊓ b) = rev a ⊔ rev b := by
  have h := rev_sup (rev a) (rev b)
  rw [rev_involutive a, rev_involutive b] at h
  calc rev (a ⊓ b) = rev (rev (rev a ⊔ rev b)) := by rw [h]
    _ = rev a ⊔ rev b := rev_involutive _

/-- The order-reversal `a ↦ 2 - a` makes the 3-chain `Fin 3` a retrocausal Heyting
algebra. Combined with `retro_lem_fails`/`retro_tem_holds` this is a concrete model in
which the law of excluded middle fails while the temporal excluded middle holds. -/
instance : RetrocausalHeyting (Fin 3) where
  rev a := 2 - a
  rev_involutive := by intro x; fin_cases x <;> rfl
  rev_antitone := by
    intro a b h
    fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp_all

/-- In the concrete `Fin 3` model, time-reversal swaps the truth poles. -/
theorem fin3_rev_swaps : rev (⊥ : Fin 3) = ⊤ ∧ rev (⊤ : Fin 3) = ⊥ :=
  ⟨rev_bot, rev_top⟩

end Retrocausal

# Chip-Firing and Divisor Theory on a Finite Graph — Definitions

This file lays the *load-bearing foundation* of Baker–Norine divisor theory on a finite
graph, working entirely over an ordinary Mathlib `SimpleGraph V`.

The central object is the **graph Laplacian** (chip-firing operator)

  `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`,

a map `(V → ℤ) → Divisor V`.  We record here the definitions (`Divisor`, `lap`,
`divisorDegree`, `genus`, `canonicalDivisor`, `Effective`, `singleVertexDivisor`,
`bnNumber`) together with the *homomorphism layer*: `lap` is additive, kills constants,
respects negation, and lands in degree zero.  These five facts are exactly the axioms
needed to make chip-firing (linear) equivalence an `Equivalence` and degree a class
invariant (developed in `Tropical.ChipFiring.Theorems`).

## References

* Baker, M. and Norine, S. "Riemann–Roch and Abel–Jacobi theory on a finite graph" (2007)

-- !-- Lab Notebook -- !--
Hypothesis: The whole algebraic layer of divisor theory is the *coset relation of one
  homomorphism* `lap`.  If `lap` is an additive, constant-killing, degree-zero map then
  linear equivalence and its degree invariance must follow purely formally.
Result: Confirmed.  `lap_zero`/`lap_neg`/`lap_add` are literally the three
  equivalence-relation axioms; `lap_deg_zero` is literally degree invariance.
Insight: `lap_deg_zero` needs *no* handshake/degree counting — it is pure antisymmetry of
  `f v − f u` under the symmetric adjacency relation, witnessed by a single
  `Finset.sum_nbij'` swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` that negates every summand.

import Mathlib

open Finset BigOperators SimpleGraph

/-! ## Divisors -/

/-- A divisor on a graph with vertex set `V` is an integer-valued function on vertices
(a formal `ℤ`-linear combination of vertices). -/
structure Divisor (V : Type*) where
  coeff : V → ℤ

namespace Divisor
variable {V : Type*}

@[ext] lemma ext {D E : Divisor V} (h : D.coeff = E.coeff) : D = E := by
  cases D; cases E; simpa using h

instance : Zero (Divisor V) := ⟨⟨fun _ => 0⟩⟩
instance : Add (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v + E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Neg (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D => ⟨fun v => -D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : Sub (Divisor V) := ⟨fun D E => ⟨fun v => D.coeff v - E.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℕ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩
instance : SMul ℤ (Divisor V) := ⟨fun n D => ⟨fun v => n • D.coeff v⟩⟩

@[simp] lemma zero_coeff (v : V) : (0 : Divisor V).coeff v = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma add_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D + E).coeff v = D.coeff v + E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma neg_coeff (D : Divisor V) (v : V) : (-D).coeff v = -D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma sub_coeff (D E : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (D - E).coeff v = D.coeff v - E.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma nsmul_coeff (n : ℕ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl
@[simp] lemma zsmul_coeff (n : ℤ) (D : Divisor V) (v : V) :
    (n • D).coeff v = n • D.coeff v := rfl

/-- The coefficient projection `Divisor V → (V → ℤ)` is injective; hence divisors form an
additive commutative group under pointwise operations. -/
instance : AddCommGroup (Divisor V) :=
  Function.Injective.addCommGroup (Divisor.coeff)
    (fun _ _ h => Divisor.ext h)
    rfl (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)
    (fun _ _ => rfl) (fun _ _ => rfl)

end Divisor

/-- A divisor is **effective** when every coefficient is non-negative. -/
def Effective {V : Type*} (D : Divisor V) : Prop := ∀ v, 0 ≤ D.coeff v

/-! ## Degree -/

section Degree
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V]

/-- The **degree** of a divisor is the sum of its coefficients. -/
def divisorDegree (D : Divisor V) : ℤ := ∑ v, D.coeff v

@[simp] lemma divisorDegree_zero : divisorDegree (0 : Divisor V) = 0 := by
  simp [divisorDegree]

lemma divisorDegree_add (D E : Divisor V) :
    divisorDegree (D + E) = divisorDegree D + divisorDegree E := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_add_distrib]

lemma divisorDegree_neg (D : Divisor V) : divisorDegree (-D) = -divisorDegree D := by
  simp [divisorDegree, Finset.sum_neg_distrib]

end Degree

/-! ## The graph Laplacian (chip-firing operator) -/

section Laplacian
variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- The graph Laplacian applied to a firing pattern `f : V → ℤ`.  Firing along `f` moves
chips according to `(lap G f).coeff v = ∑_{u ∼ v} (f v − f u)`. -/
def lap (f : V → ℤ) : Divisor V := ⟨fun v => ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u)⟩

@[simp] lemma lap_coeff (f : V → ℤ) (v : V) :
    (lap G f).coeff v = ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u) := rfl

-- !-- The empty firing pattern moves no chips: each summand `0 - 0` vanishes. -- !--
@[simp] theorem lap_zero : lap G (0 : V → ℤ) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- A constant firing pattern is in the kernel: every summand `c - c` vanishes. -- !--
theorem lap_const (c : ℤ) : lap G (fun _ => c) = 0 := by
  ext v; simp

-- !-- Additivity: `(f+g)v - (f+g)u = (f v - f u) + (g v - g u)`, then split the sum. -- !--
theorem lap_add (f g : V → ℤ) : lap G (f + g) = lap G f + lap G g := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.add_coeff, Pi.add_apply, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Negation: `lap` is `ℤ`-linear, so it commutes with pointwise negation. -- !--
theorem lap_neg (f : V → ℤ) : lap G (-f) = - lap G f := by
  ext v
  simp only [lap_coeff, Divisor.neg_coeff, Pi.neg_apply, ← Finset.sum_neg_distrib]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl; intro u _; ring

-- !-- Every Laplacian has degree zero, by antisymmetry of `f v - f u` under the symmetric
--     adjacency relation: the swap `(v,u) ↦ (u,v)` on adjacent ordered pairs negates each
--     summand yet preserves the index set, forcing `X = -X`. -- !--
theorem lap_deg_zero (f : V → ℤ) : divisorDegree (lap G f) = 0 := by
  unfold divisorDegree
  simp only [lap_coeff]
  have key : (∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f v - f u))
      = ∑ v, ∑ u ∈ G.neighborFinset v, (f u - f v) := by
    rw [Finset.sum_sigma', Finset.sum_sigma']
    apply Finset.sum_nbij' (fun x => (⟨x.2, x.1⟩ : Σ _ : V, V)) (fun x => ⟨x.2, x.1⟩)
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ h
      simp only [Finset.mem_sigma, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, mem_neighborFinset] at *
      exact h.symm
    · rintro ⟨v, u⟩ _; rfl

# Future Directions — CSS Codes as Cohomology

This cycle established the dictionary **CSS code = homology of an `F₂`-chain
complex** (`Core.lean`), *refuted* the hypercube conjecture for the 1-skeleton
cycle code (`CubeCode.lean`), and anchored the refutation with a fully explicit
`[[4,1]]` code on `C₄ = Q₂` (`RingCode.lean`). The surviving topological
invariant is the cyclomatic number `β₁(Q_n) = (n−2)·2^{n-1} + 1`, which equals
`1` **only** at `n = 2`. The directions below grow out of exactly those findings.

---

## Conjecture 1 — The cube becomes a `[[·,1,·]]` code only after filling 2-cells

For the *cubical* complex `Q_n` (vertices, edges **and** square 2-faces), the
homological code has `k = dim H₁(Q_n; F₂) = 0` for `n ≥ 2` (the cube is simply
connected), so to recover a single logical qubit one must quotient/identify
faces into a closed surface. Concretely: there is a surface `Σ` obtained from
`Q_n`'s 2-skeleton with `dim H₁(Σ; F₂) = 1` and code distance equal to the
girth `4`, **not** `2^{n/2}`.

- **The key insight is** that the mission's "1 qubit" claim silently assumes a
  *surface* (2-complex) where 2-cells kill all but one homology class, while the
  literal `Z₁/B₁` cycle code on the 1-skeleton has `B₁ = 0` and therefore
  over-encodes by the full cyclomatic number `(n−2)2^{n-1}+1`.
- **Why now?** `CubeCode.numLogical_graphCode` already isolates the `d₂ = 0`
  (no-2-cell) case; adding a nonzero `d₂` for the square faces is a direct,
  mechanical extension of the same `Core` dimension formula, so the surface vs.
  graph dichotomy is immediately testable in the existing framework.

## Conjecture 2 — Homological distance is governed by Hamming weight, and the cube saturates only the trivial Singleton bound

Define the code distance `d` as the minimum `hammingWeight` (already imported
from the catalog's `vecSupport`) over nonzero homology representatives. Then for
the `C₄` code `d = 4`, and every cube 1-skeleton code has `d = girth = 4`,
giving `k + d = β₁ + 4`, which violates the quantum Singleton bound
`k + 2d ≤ n + 2` for large `n` — i.e. the 1-skeleton codes are **bad** codes,
the opposite of the conjecture's "achieves the Singleton bound" claim.

- **The key insight is** that distance is a *minimum-weight* invariant of the
  cohomology class, so the catalog's `vecSupport_card_pos_of_ne_zero` is the
  exact primitive needed, and the constant girth `4` forces asymptotically
  vanishing relative distance `d/n → 0`.
- **Why now?** `RingCode.ker_boundary` shows the homology class explicitly as a
  single weight-4 vector; computing `hammingWeight` of a kernel basis is already
  `decide`-feasible at small `n`, so the Singleton-violation can be certified
  before any general theory is built.

## Conjecture 3 — `β₁(Q_n) = 1 ⇔ n = 2` is the only finite-qubit cube; tori are the right family

Replacing `Q_n` by the discrete torus `(C_m)^{×2}` (product of two `m`-cycles)
as a 2-complex yields `dim H₁ = 2` (the toric code) with distance `m`, the
genuine `[[2m², 2, m]]` family. Conjecture: among all "graph-cube-like" 1-complexes,
`β₁ = 1` characterizes `C₄` uniquely, and the *only* way to keep `k` bounded
while growing `n` is to add 2-cells (move to a surface).

- **The key insight is** that `cube_one_qubit_iff` pins `k = 1` to `n = 2` for
  the cube, so bounded-`k` code families must come from *surfaces of fixed
  genus*, not from growing graphs — exactly the toric-code construction.
- **Why now?** The closed form `cyclomatic_closed_form` makes the `k`-growth
  exact, so contrasting it against the constant `k = 2` of a torus 2-complex is a
  clean, fully arithmetic comparison reusing the present `cyclomatic` machinery.

## Conjecture 4 — Euler characteristic is the universal qubit budget

For any bounded `F₂`-chain complex `0 → Cₖ → ⋯ → C₀ → 0`, the alternating sum of
homology dimensions equals the alternating sum of chain dimensions
(`∑ (−1)ⁱ dim Hᵢ = ∑ (−1)ⁱ dim Cᵢ = χ`). Hence the *total* logical-qubit budget
across all degrees of a chain-complex code is the topological Euler
characteristic, a single integer invariant.

- **The key insight is** that `Core.finrank_homology` already expresses one
  homology dimension as a difference of ranks; iterating rank–nullity up the
  complex telescopes into `χ`, so "qubits = Euler characteristic" is a
  rank–nullity identity, not new analysis.
- **Why now?** `Core` proves the single-spot case with `finrank_quotient_add_finrank`;
  the multi-degree version is the same lemma applied inductively, well within the
  subagent's reach.

## Conjecture 5 — Every classical `[n,k]` `F₂` code is the degree-0 homology of a length-1 complex, making CSS ↔ classical functorial

For a parity-check map `H : F₂ⁿ → F₂^r`, the length-1 complex `F₂ⁿ →H F₂^r` has
`H₀ = coker H` and `H₁ = ker H = ` the classical code, with `dim H₁ = n − rank H`.
Conjecture: the assignment `(C₁, C₂) ↦ (chain complex)` and back is an
equivalence of categories between CSS codes and bounded `F₂`-chain complexes up
to chain homotopy.

- **The key insight is** that `numLogical_eq_css` is precisely the object-level
  half of this equivalence (`k = n − rank H_Z − rank H_X`); promoting it to a
  functor only requires tracking chain maps, which Mathlib's `HomologicalComplex`
  already supports.
- **Why now?** With the dimension dictionary proved and the cube/`C₄` examples in
  hand, the remaining work is purely categorical bookkeeping on top of existing
  `Core` definitions — no new hard analytic input is needed.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Fixed points of elementary cellular automata over `GF(2)`

We study elementary cellular automata (ECA) acting on *cyclic* arrays
`s : Fin n → ZMod 2`.  A local rule is a function
`g : ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2` taking the (left, center, right) values of a
cell and producing the new center value.  The induced global map `step g` updates
every cell simultaneously using cyclic neighbours, and a configuration `s` is a
*fixed point* when `step g s = s`.

We give complete fixed–point classifications and exact cardinalities for a small set
of Wolfram rules expressed by explicit `ZMod 2` formulas:

* Rule 204 — identity (`g204 a b c = b`): **every** configuration is fixed; there are
  `2 ^ n` of them.
* Rule 0 — constant zero (`g0 a b c = 0`): the unique fixed point is the zero
  configuration; there is `1`.
* Rule 51 — complement (`g51 a b c = 1 + b`): for `n ≥ 1` there are **no** fixed
  points.
* Rule 90 — XOR of neighbours (`g90 a b c = a + c`): a configuration is fixed iff it
  satisfies the GF(2) recurrence `s i = s (i-1) + s (i+1)` for all `i`.  We prove every
  such configuration is `3`-periodic, and that the number of fixed points is
  `4` when `3 ∣ n` and `1` otherwise.

## A note on the original speculative motivation

This file deliberately does **not** pursue the original claim relating automaton
"complexity" to an algebraic-geometric "fixed-point dimension".  Instead it provides a
concrete counterexample to that intuition: Rule 204 and Rule 0 are both as simple as
possible, yet Rule 204 has the *maximal* fixed-point set (`2 ^ n`) while Rule 0 has the
*minimal* nonempty one (`1`).  Likewise the linear Rule 90 has only `1` fixed point for
most lengths.  Thus the size of the fixed-point set does not track any reasonable notion
of dynamical complexity.

The prompt suggested the Rule 90 fixed count is `2 ^ gcd n 2` and that fixed points
coincide with the `2`-periodic configurations.  This is **false** for the standard
Rule 90 local map `g90 a b c = a + c`: e.g. for `n = 2` every configuration is
`2`-periodic but only the zero configuration is fixed.  The set counted by
`2 ^ gcd n 2` is the set of `2`-periodic configurations, which is genuinely different
from the fixed-point set of Rule 90.  The corrected statement proved below is that the
Rule 90 fixed count is `4` when `3 ∣ n` and `1` otherwise.
-/

namespace ECAFixedPoints

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- Cyclic left neighbour on `Fin n` (predecessor, wrapping around). -/
def leftN [NeZero n] (i : Fin n) : Fin n := i - 1

/-- Cyclic right neighbour on `Fin n` (successor, wrapping around). -/
def rightN [NeZero n] (i : Fin n) : Fin n := i + 1

/-- The global update map induced by a local rule `g`, using cyclic neighbours. -/
def step [NeZero n] (g : ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2)
    (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) : Fin n → ZMod 2 :=
  fun i => g (s (leftN i)) (s i) (s (rightN i))

/-- A configuration `s` is a fixed point of the rule `g` when `step g s = s`. -/
def isFixed [NeZero n] (g : ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2)
    (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) : Prop := step g s = s

/-- Rule 204: identity local rule. -/
def g204 (_a b _c : ZMod 2) : ZMod 2 := b

/-- Rule 0: constant zero local rule. -/
def g0 (_a _b _c : ZMod 2) : ZMod 2 := 0

/-- Rule 51: complement local rule (`1 + b` over `ZMod 2`). -/
def g51 (_a b _c : ZMod 2) : ZMod 2 := 1 + b

/-- Rule 90: XOR of the two neighbours. -/
def g90 (a _b c : ZMod 2) : ZMod 2 := a + c

/-! ### Basic unfolding -/

theorem step_apply [NeZero n] (g : ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2)
    (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) (i : Fin n) :
    step g s i = g (s (i - 1)) (s i) (s (i + 1)) := rfl

theorem isFixed_iff [NeZero n] (g : ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2)
    (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) :
    isFixed g s ↔ ∀ i, g (s (i - 1)) (s i) (s (i + 1)) = s i := by
  simp only [isFixed, step, leftN, rightN, funext_iff]

/-! ### Rule 204 : every configuration is fixed -/

theorem isFixed_g204 [NeZero n] (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) : isFixed g204 s := by
  funext i
  rfl

/-! ### Rule 0 : only the zero configuration is fixed -/

theorem isFixed_g0_iff [NeZero n] (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) :
    isFixed g0 s ↔ s = 0 := by
  rw [isFixed_iff]
  constructor
  · intro h
    funext i
    simpa [g0, eq_comm] using h i
  · intro h
    subst h
    intro i
    simp [g0]

/-! ### Rule 51 : no configuration is fixed -/

theorem not_isFixed_g51 [NeZero n] (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) : ¬ isFixed g51 s := by
  rw [isFixed_iff]
  intro h
  have hi := h (0 : Fin n)
  simp only [g51] at hi
  -- `1 + s 0 = s 0` is impossible in `ZMod 2`
  have : (1 : ZMod 2) = 0 := by linear_combination hi
  exact one_ne_zero this

/-! ### Rule 90 : characterization and periodicity -/

theorem isFixed_g90_iff [NeZero n] (s : Fin n → ZMod 2) :
    isFixed g90 s ↔ ∀ i, s i = s (i - 1) + s (i + 1) := by
  rw [isFixed_iff]
  constructor
  · intro h i; exact (h i).symm
  · intro h i; exact (h i).symm

/-- Every Rule 90 fixed configuration is `3`-periodic. -/
theorem g90_period3 [NeZero n] {s : Fin n → ZMod 2} (hf : isFixed g90 s) :
    ∀ i, s (i + 1 + 1 + 1) = s i := by
  rw [isFixed_g90_iff] at hf
  intro i
  have lem : ∀ A B C D : ZMod 2, A = B + C → C = A + D → D = B := by decide
  have h1 := hf (i + 1)
  have h2 := hf (i + 1 + 1)
  rw [show (i + 1) - 1 = i by abel] at h1
  rw [show (i + 1 + 1) - 1 = i + 1 by abel] at h2
  exact lem _ _ _ _ h1 h2

/-! ### Cardinalities -/

/-- Rule 204: the fixed-point set is everything, so it has `2 ^ n` elements. -/
theorem card_fixed_g204 [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card {s : Fin n → ZMod 2 // isFixed g204 s} = 2 ^ n := by
  simp +decide [ isFixed_g204 ]

/-- Rule 0: the unique fixed point is the zero configuration. -/
theorem card_fixed_g0 [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card {s : Fin n → ZMod 2 // isFixed g0 s} = 1 := by
  rw [ Nat.card_eq_one_iff_unique ];
  exact ⟨ by exact ⟨ fun x y => by ext; exact ( isFixed_g0_iff _ ).1 x.2 ▸ ( isFixed_g0_iff _ ).1 y.2 ▸ rfl ⟩, ⟨ 0, isFixed_g0_iff _ |>.2 rfl ⟩ ⟩

/-- Rule 51: for `n ≥ 1` there are no fixed points. -/
theorem card_fixed_g51 [NeZero n] :
    Nat.card {s : Fin n → ZMod 2 // isFixed g51 s} = 0 := by
  rw [ Nat.card_eq_zero, isEmpty_subtype ];
  exact Or.inl fun x => not_isFixed_g51 x

/-! #### Rule 90 cardinality -/

/-- When `3 ∤ n`, the only Rule 90 fixed point is the zero configuration. -/
theorem g90_eq_zero_of_not_dvd [NeZero n] (h3 : ¬ (3 ∣ n))
    {s : Fin n → ZMod 2} (hf : isFixed g90 s) : s = 0 := by
  -- By induction on $k$, we get $∀ i, s (i + (3*k : (Fin n))) = s i$.
  have h_ind : ∀ k : ℕ, ∀ i : Fin n, s (i + (k • (1 + 1 + 1) : Fin n)) = s i := by
    intro k i; induction' k with k ih <;> simp_all +decide [ ← add_assoc ] ;
    have := g90_period3 hf ( i + k • 1 + k • 1 + k • 1 ) ; simp_all +decide [ add_assoc ] ;
    convert this using 2 ; norm_num [ add_smul, Fin.add_def ] ; ring_nf;
  -- Since `¬ 3 ∣ n` and `3` is prime, `Nat.Coprime 3 n`, so `3` is invertible mod `n`.
  obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ : ∃ m : ℕ, m * 3 ≡ 1 [MOD n] := by
    have := Nat.exists_mul_mod_eq_one_of_coprime ( show Nat.Coprime 3 n from Nat.prime_three.coprime_iff_not_dvd.mpr h3 );
    rcases n with ( _ | _ | n ) <;> simp_all +decide [ mul_comm, Nat.ModEq ];
    · exists 0;
    · exact ⟨ this.choose, this.choose_spec.2 ⟩;
  -- Taking `k = m`, the shift by `3*m` equals the shift by `1` in `Fin n` (because `3*m ≡ 1 (mod n)`), giving `∀ i, s (i + 1) = s i`.
  have h_shift : ∀ i : Fin n, s (i + 1) = s i := by
    convert h_ind m using 3;
    norm_num [ Fin.add_def, Fin.mul_def ];
    simp_all +decide [ ← ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff' ];
    erw [ Fin.val_mk ] ; norm_cast ; simp_all +decide [ ← ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff ];
    erw [ show ( nsmulRec m ⟨ 3 % n, Nat.mod_lt _ <| NeZero.pos n ⟩ : Fin n ) = ⟨ ( m * 3 ) % n, Nat.mod_lt _ <| NeZero.pos n ⟩ from ?_ ] ; aesop;
    refine' Nat.recOn m _ _ <;> simp_all +decide [ nsmulRec ];
    simp +decide [ Fin.add_def, Nat.succ_mul ];
  -- From `s (i+1) = s i` for all `i` we also get `s (i-1) = s i` (apply at `i-1` and simplify `i-1+1 = i`).
  have h_prev : ∀ i : Fin n, s (i - 1) = s i := by
    exact fun i => by rw [ ← h_shift ] ; simp +decide ;
  ext i; have := hf; simp_all +decide [ isFixed_iff ] ;
  specialize hf i; simp_all +decide [ g90 ] ;

/-- The `3`-periodic configuration with residue-classes `a, b, a+b`. -/
def decode3 (a b : ZMod 2) : Fin n → ZMod 2 :=
  fun i => if i.val % 3 = 0 then a else if i.val % 3 = 1 then b else a + b

/-- When `3 ∣ n`, the residue mod `3` of the cyclic successor index. -/
theorem succ_val_mod_three [NeZero n] (h3 : 3 ∣ n) (i : Fin n) :
    (i + 1).val % 3 = (i.val + 1) % 3 := by
  obtain ⟨ k, hk ⟩ := h3;
  norm_num [ Fin.val_add, Nat.add_mod, Nat.mul_mod, hk ]

/-- When `3 ∣ n`, the residue mod `3` of the cyclic predecessor index. -/
theorem pred_val_mod_three [NeZero n] (h3 : 3 ∣ n) (i : Fin n) :
    (i - 1).val % 3 = (i.val + 2) % 3 := by
  -- Since $3 \mid n$, we have $n \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$.
  have hn_mod : n % 3 = 0 := by
    exact Nat.mod_eq_zero_of_dvd h3;

/-!
# Retrocausal Heyting Algebras: Where Effects Precede Causes

This module formalizes **retrocausal logical structures**, where an order-reversing
involution (a "time-reversal" / CPT operator) models implications flowing *backward*
in time. The central phenomena are:

* **The law of excluded middle (LEM) fails** in genuinely intuitionistic (non-Boolean)
  Heyting algebras (`retro_lem_fails`).
* **A temporal excluded middle (TEM) always holds**: the *double negation* of LEM is
  valid in *every* Heyting algebra (`temporal_excluded_middle`). This is the Glivenko /
  weak-excluded-middle phenomenon reinterpreted temporally: `¬¬(a ∨ ¬a) = ⊤`.
* **Any retrocausal logic must be intuitionistic**: rejecting LEM is *equivalent* to
  rejecting double-negation elimination (`lem_iff_dne`). Hence a logic that admits a
  proper retrocausal (non-Boolean) structure cannot be classical.
* A retrocausal **time-reversal** is an antitone involution; it satisfies De Morgan
  dualities `rev (a ⊔ b) = rev a ⊓ rev b` and swaps `⊥ ↔ ⊤` (`rev_sup`, `rev_inf`,
  `rev_bot`, `rev_top`).

namespace Retrocausal

/-! ## Part I. The temporal excluded middle (TEM) -/

/-- **Temporal excluded middle.** In *every* Heyting algebra the *double negation* of
the law of excluded middle holds: `¬¬(a ∨ ¬a) = ⊤`. Intuitionistically LEM may fail,
but its temporal (doubly-negated) shadow always survives — effects may precede causes
without contradiction. -/
theorem temporal_excluded_middle {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α] (a : α) :
    (a ⊔ aᶜ)ᶜᶜ = ⊤ := by
  have h : (a ⊔ aᶜ)ᶜ = ⊥ := by rw [compl_sup_distrib, inf_compl_eq_bot]
  rw [h, compl_bot]

/-- **LEM ⟺ double-negation elimination.** The law of excluded middle holds for every
element iff double negation can be eliminated for every element. Hence *rejecting* LEM is
equivalent to *rejecting* DNE: any logic without LEM is genuinely intuitionistic.

The backward direction reuses `temporal_excluded_middle`: DNE turns the always-valid
doubly-negated LEM back into honest LEM. -/
theorem lem_iff_dne {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α] :
    (∀ a : α, a ⊔ aᶜ = ⊤) ↔ (∀ a : α, aᶜᶜ = a) := by
  constructor
  · intro hlem a
    have hd : aᶜᶜ ⊓ (a ⊔ aᶜ) = (aᶜᶜ ⊓ a) ⊔ (aᶜᶜ ⊓ aᶜ) := inf_sup_left _ _ _
    rw [hlem a, inf_top_eq] at hd
    have h2 : aᶜᶜ ⊓ aᶜ = ⊥ := by rw [inf_comm]; exact inf_compl_eq_bot
    rw [h2, sup_bot_eq, inf_comm, inf_eq_left.mpr le_compl_compl] at hd
    exact hd
  · intro hdne a
    have h : (a ⊔ aᶜ)ᶜᶜ = ⊤ := temporal_excluded_middle a
    rw [hdne] at h; exact h

/-- **Retrocausal logic must be intuitionistic (contrapositive form).** If LEM fails for
some element, then double-negation elimination must fail for some element too. -/
theorem lem_fails_of_dne_fails {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α]
    (h : ∃ a : α, aᶜᶜ ≠ a) : ∃ a : α, a ⊔ aᶜ ≠ ⊤ := by
  by_contra hc
  push_neg at hc
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h
  exact ha (lem_iff_dne.mp hc a)

/-- **Concrete failure of LEM.** The three-element chain `Fin 3` is a genuinely
non-Boolean Heyting algebra: for the middle element `1`, `1 ⊔ 1ᶜ = 1 ≠ ⊤`. This is the
existence witness backing the abstract `lem_fails_of_dne_fails`. -/
theorem retro_lem_fails : ∃ a : Fin 3, a ⊔ aᶜ ≠ ⊤ := ⟨1, by decide⟩

/-- The temporal excluded middle nevertheless holds at that same witness in `Fin 3`. -/
theorem retro_tem_holds : ((1 : Fin 3) ⊔ (1 : Fin 3)ᶜ)ᶜᶜ = ⊤ :=
  temporal_excluded_middle 1

/-! ## Part II. Retrocausal time-reversal -/

/-- A **retrocausal time-reversal** on a Heyting algebra is an order-*reversing*
involution `rev`. Order reversal encodes "implications flowing backward in time":
`a ≤ b` (cause `a` entails effect `b`) becomes `rev b ≤ rev a` under time reversal.
Involutivity is the algebraic shadow of the CPT theorem (`(CPT)² = id`). -/
class RetrocausalHeyting (α : Type*) [HeytingAlgebra α] where
  /-- The time-reversal / CPT operator. -/
  rev : α → α
  /-- Time reversal is an involution: applying it twice is the identity. -/
  rev_involutive : Function.Involutive rev
  /-- Time reversal reverses entailment (implications flow backward). -/
  rev_antitone : ∀ {a b : α}, a ≤ b → rev b ≤ rev a

export RetrocausalHeyting (rev rev_involutive rev_antitone)

variable {α : Type*} [HeytingAlgebra α] [RetrocausalHeyting α]

/-- Time reversal sends contradiction to tautology: `rev ⊥ = ⊤`. -/
theorem rev_bot : rev (⊥ : α) = ⊤ := by
  apply top_le_iff.mp
  have h := rev_antitone (bot_le : (⊥ : α) ≤ rev ⊤)
  rwa [rev_involutive ⊤] at h

/-- Time reversal sends tautology to contradiction: `rev ⊤ = ⊥`. -/
theorem rev_top : rev (⊤ : α) = ⊥ := by
  apply le_bot_iff.mp
  have h := rev_antitone (le_top : rev ⊥ ≤ (⊤ : α))
  rwa [rev_involutive ⊥] at h

/-- **De Morgan for time-reversal.** A retrocausal involution turns joins into meets:
`rev (a ⊔ b) = rev a ⊓ rev b`. -/
theorem rev_sup (a b : α) : rev (a ⊔ b) = rev a ⊓ rev b := by
  apply le_antisymm
  · exact le_inf (rev_antitone le_sup_left) (rev_antitone le_sup_right)
  · have h1 : a ≤ rev (rev a ⊓ rev b) := by
      have h := rev_antitone (inf_le_left : rev a ⊓ rev b ≤ rev a)
      rwa [rev_involutive a] at h
    have h2 : b ≤ rev (rev a ⊓ rev b) := by
      have h := rev_antitone (inf_le_right : rev a ⊓ rev b ≤ rev b)
      rwa [rev_involutive b] at h
    have h3 := rev_antitone (sup_le h1 h2)
    rwa [rev_involutive (rev a ⊓ rev b)] at h3

/-- **Dual De Morgan for time-reversal.** A retrocausal involution turns meets into
joins: `rev (a ⊓ b) = rev a ⊔ rev b`. -/
theorem rev_inf (a b : α) : rev (a ⊓ b) = rev a ⊔ rev b := by
  have h := rev_sup (rev a) (rev b)
  rw [rev_involutive a, rev_involutive b] at h
  calc rev (a ⊓ b) = rev (rev (rev a ⊔ rev b)) := by rw [h]
    _ = rev a ⊔ rev b := rev_involutive _

/-! ## Part III. A concrete retrocausal Heyting algebra with failing LEM -/

/-- The order-reversal `a ↦ 2 - a` makes the 3-chain `Fin 3` a retrocausal Heyting
algebra. Combined with `retro_lem_fails`/`retro_tem_holds` this is a concrete model in
which the law of excluded middle fails while the temporal excluded middle holds. -/
instance : RetrocausalHeyting (Fin 3) where
  rev a := 2 - a
  rev_involutive := by intro x; fin_cases x <;> rfl
  rev_antitone := by
    intro a b h
    fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp_all

/-- In the concrete `Fin 3` model, time-reversal swaps the truth poles. -/
theorem fin3_rev_swaps : rev (⊥ : Fin 3) = ⊤ ∧ rev (⊤ : Fin 3) = ⊥ :=
  ⟨rev_bot, rev_top⟩

end Retrocausal

# Future Directions — Cellular Automata as Algebraic Geometry over GF(2)

These conjectures are distilled from the v16a research cycle in
`Computation/ECAFixedVariety.lean` and `Computation/ECALinearSubspace.lean`.

The cycle established two anchor facts:

* **Refutation.** The Turing-complete Wolfram Rule 110 has a *single* fixed point
  (the all-zero configuration) for every length `n ≥ 1`, hence fixed-point-variety
  dimension `0` — the *minimum* among nonempty varieties — directly falsifying the
  conjecture "Turing-complete ⇒ maximal fixed-point dimension"
  (`complexity_dimension_conjecture_false`).
* **Structure.** For *linear* (additive) rules the fixed-point set is literally the
  kernel of `step − id`, a `GF(2)`-subspace, so it always has `2^k` points
  (`linearFixed_card_pow_two`); Rule 110 is provably nonlinear (`g110_not_linear`).

The fixed-point variety is therefore a real GF(2) scheme, but its dimension is the
*wrong* complexity invariant. The directions below propose the right one.

---

## Direction 1 — Spacetime entropy, not fixed-point dimension, tracks complexity.

**Conjecture.** Define the *spacetime subshift* `Σ_r` of rule `r` as the set of valid
bi-infinite orbit diagrams, an SFT over the de Bruijn graph. Its topological entropy
`h(Σ_r) = lim (1/n) log #(period-n columns)` separates Wolfram's classes:
`h = 0` for Class 1/2, `h > 0` for Class 3, and Class 4 (e.g. Rule 110) sits exactly
at the `h = 0` boundary while supporting unbounded transients.

**The key insight is** that Turing-completeness lives in the *transient orbit
structure* (gliders, collisions), which the static fixed-point variety throws away;
the spacetime SFT retains it and its entropy is the genuine invariant.

**Why now?** This cycle proved the fixed-point count of Rule 110 is constantly `1`,
so any complexity invariant *must* be orbit-based, not equilibrium-based. The
transfer-matrix machinery for counting period-`n` configurations (`tr(T^n)`) is
already formalizable in Mathlib (`Matrix.trace`, `Matrix.pow`), giving an immediate
attack route.

## Direction 2 — Fixed-point count is `tr(Tᵣⁿ)` for a 4×4 GF(2)-transfer matrix.

**Conjecture.** For every rule `r` there is an explicit `0/1` matrix `T_r` indexed by
2-cell windows such that `Nat.card {s : Config n // isFixed (g r) s} = trace (T_rⁿ)`,
and the asymptotic growth rate equals the Perron eigenvalue `ρ(T_r)`; the variety
"dimension" is `log₂ ρ(T_r)`, a rule-intrinsic real number.

**The key insight is** that the fixed-point set is a *subshift of finite type*, so its
cardinality is governed by a transfer matrix exactly as in statistical mechanics —
turning a combinatorial count into linear algebra.

**Why now?** We verified the pattern computationally (Rule 90: `1,1,4,1,1,4,…`,
period-3 because `ρ` has a cube-root-of-unity spectrum; Rule 204: `2^n` because
`ρ = 2`). Proving `#fix = tr(Tⁿ)` for the five formalized rules is a finite, bounded
target that would convert every numeric observation in the Lab Notes into a theorem.

## Direction 3 — `3 ∣ n ⇔ Rule 90 has a nonzero fixed point`.

**Conjecture.** The Rule 90 fixed-point subspace `linearFixed 1 0 1` over `Config n`
has dimension `> 0` if and only if `3 ∣ n`; equivalently the circulant operator
`x ↦ x_{i-1} + x_{i+1} − x_i` is singular over `GF(2)` exactly when `3 ∣ n`. More
generally the dimension equals `deg gcd(t² + t + 1, tⁿ − 1)` in `GF(2)[t]`.

**The key insight is** that a linear ECA's fixed-point dimension is a *cyclotomic*
quantity: it counts roots of the rule's characteristic polynomial among the `n`-th
roots of unity, so number theory (orders mod small primes) governs the geometry.

**Why now?** We proved a nonzero fixed point exists at `n = 3`
(`rule90_nontrivial_fixed_three`) and `linearFixed_card_pow_two` already exposes the
dimension as `finrank`. Mathlib's `Polynomial.cyclotomic` and circulant-matrix
support make the gcd characterization directly reachable.

## Direction 4 — Linearity is *decidable from the variety* up to the converse gap.

**Conjecture.** A rule `r` is GF(2)-linear iff its fixed-point variety is closed under
addition for *all* lengths `n` simultaneously; a single length can fail (the converse
gap noted by the Critic: Rule 0 and Rule 110 both give count `1 = 2⁰` yet only Rule 0
is linear). Precisely: `(∀ n, IsSubmodule (fixed r n)) ↔ r ∈ {0,60,90,102,150,170,204,240,…}`
(the 8 additive rules and their reflections).

**The key insight is** that linearity is a *global* property of the whole tower of
varieties `{V_n}`, not of any single `V_n` — closure-at-one-`n` is necessary but not
sufficient, which is why our safe-direction lemma (`g110_not_linear`) certifies
nonlinearity pointwise rather than from a single count.

**Why now?** This cycle isolated the exact converse counterexample (count `1` is
realized by both a linear and a nonlinear rule), so the precise boundary is known and
ready to be formalized as an `Iff` over the finite catalogue of additive rules.

## Direction 5 — Affine rules give *cosets*; the empty variety detects an inhomogeneity.

**Conjecture.** A rule with affine ANF `f = ℓ(a,b,c) + 1` (a linear part plus the
constant `1`, e.g. Rule 51 `= b + 1`) has fixed-point variety either empty or a
*coset* of `linearFixed ℓ`; it is empty exactly when `1 ∉ image(ℓ − id)`. Thus the
empty variety (`rule51_not_isFixed`) is the GF(2) shadow of an unsolvable affine
system, and `#fix ∈ {0} ∪ {2^k}`.

**The key insight is** that the constant term in the ANF turns the *kernel* (subspace)
into an *affine* solution set, so the dichotomy "empty vs. power-of-two coset" is the
Rouché–Capelli theorem over `GF(2)` applied to cellular automata.

**Why now?** We already proved Rule 51's variety is empty for all `n`; recasting that
as the inconsistency of an affine GF(2) system, via Mathlib's `LinearMap.range` and
coset API, would unify the linear (Direction 1–3) and degenerate cases under one
solvability criterion.
